title: POC Weekly Sync - App Integration: SDK/tool/function/structured output
summary: Weekly POC sync reviewing SDK integration progress for payments reconciliation assistant. Covered function/tool calling patterns, structured-output JSON schema, initial benchmark results (latency/cost), error handling and telemetry, and security questions (VPC, KMS, audit logs). Agreed next steps: share sample repo + integration guide, run larger perf runs, set up short dedicated trial for baseline, and follow up with security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to share sample SDK integration repo and structured-output examples (Maya)
SE to run perf benchmarks at 256/512 token lengths and upload spreadsheet (Daniel)
LumenPay to send representative payloads and success criteria (Aisha)
Schedule performance deep-dive next week to review benchmark diffs and tuning (all)
action_items: Maya: share integration guide + sample repo by 2026-08-03
Daniel: run perf tests (256/512 tokens) and post spreadsheet by 2026-08-06
Aisha: provide example payloads, privacy redaction notes, and success criteria by 2026-08-05
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a minute. we're at the weekly POC sync for the reconciliation assistant, 45 minutes on the calendar.
[00:14] Aisha: yep thanks, we got some items from engineering to go through, mainly around the SDK and the function calling patterns.
[00:32] Daniel: quick status from our side — we reviewed the SDK integration you sent, ran the basic end-to-end, function-calls are working but we saw some mismatch on the structured-output schema in a couple of dead paths.
[00:48] Marco: when you say mismatch, is that schema validation failing server-side or just parsing on our end?
[00:55] Daniel: mostly parsing — the SDK returned a close-to-valid JSON but some keys were null or spelled slightly different, like "txn_id" vs "transactionId" — small stuff but it breaks our downstream strict typed parser.
[01:10] Maya: yep this is expected early on; we suggested using the SDK's schema enforcement helper — the "validateSchema" utility — which can coerce common variants and produces a warning trace so you can see which fields got normalized. we'll share examples.
[01:28] Linda: is that part of the hosted API or the SDK? we prefer normalization client-side to avoid changing production data.
[01:36] Maya: the helper is in the SDK and runs client-side; we also have optional server-side post-processing on Redwood Dedicated if you want stronger enforcement.
[01:45] Aisha: okay good. next, tool calls: we tried wiring the payments-lookup tool and the function-calls for enrichment. sometimes the tool call stalls and returns a generic error, looks like timeout.
[02:02] Daniel: can you paste the exact trace? timeouts are typically either network or we hit the routing fallback to a cheaper model; that can add time while the runtime switches variants.
[02:16] Aisha: sample: "tool_call error: timeout after 10s; fallback invoked". we set the default timeout to 10s in our adapter.
[02:25] Daniel: right — by default SDK uses 10s. for your latency SLO we might bump to 20s or pin the route to Dedicated capacity which avoids variant fallback. Dedicated will be faster and more predictable but costlier.
[02:39] Marco: what's the rough delta? Dedicated vs hosted?
[02:42] Maya: ballpark — hosted has variable p99 depending on load, maybe 300–700ms per token in our observed runs; Dedicated you can expect 20–30% lower p95 and far more consistent p99. cost wise, Dedicated is a committed resource, so unit token cost can be similar or slightly lower if you use batching and caching optimally. we'll put numbers in the spreadsheet.
[03:00] Linda: caching — can we cache lookups? we have a lot of repeated merchant ids.
[03:06] Daniel: yes, automatic prefix + KV cache helps a lot for repeated prompts. Our runtime supports a per-route KV-cache, and SDK exposes a cache key helper. downside: cache warmup and staleness; for reconciliation you probably want short TTLs.
[03:23] Aisha: noted. structured output: we need strict JSON output with an errors array and field-level confidence. is there an opinionated pattern you recommend?
[03:33] Maya: we usually do a top-level {"result": {...}, "errors": [...], "meta": {"confidence": ...}} shape. we also support a compact schema for lower token overhead. with structured-output mode the runtime will try to keep tokens minimal and we can validate against a provided JSON schema before returning.
[03:52] Marco: does that validation add latency?
[03:55] Daniel: small overhead, typically 10–30ms for the validation pass, depends on schema complexity. if you're tight on latency we can do async validation and surface warnings; or validate only on a sample.
[04:09] Aisha: about function signatures: currently we send functions as signature + params, but sometimes the model returns with additional keys. how do we handle forward compatibility?
[04:19] Maya: good question — recommended pattern is to accept and log unknown keys (don't fail), and include a version field in the schema. SDK's helper will strip unknown fields or keep them in an "extra" object, whichever you prefer.
[04:33] Linda: security — quick check, we need KMS integration and audit logs for any PII. where are these documented?
[04:40] Maya: we have an enterprise security pack: KMS/HSM integration, configurable audit logs (per-request), SOC2 + ISO docs. for Private deployments we can do a VPC-only control plane and customer-managed KMS. I'll attach the security pack links after the call.
[04:57] Marco: do those audit logs include token-level cost breakdowns?
[05:02] Daniel: yes we emit token usage and latency per call in the trace — can be routed to your SIEM.
[05:09] Aisha: back to perf — we ran a small batch: 1000 requests at 128 tokens, average latency 420ms and p95~1.1s, cost QPS was low. but when we increased to 512 tokens the p95 jumped to 2.8s and cost per request rose ~3x. any tuning knobs?
[05:30] Daniel: sequence length effects are expected. options: quantized model variants for cheaper per-token compute, dynamic batching, and smaller context windows for prompts via retrieval. also try prefix/KV cache to avoid re-sending context; and you can enable streaming so UI sees partial results sooner.
[05:47] Marco: can we benchmark quantized models in the pilot?
[05:50] Maya: yes, we can spin up a quantized variant on Dedicated for a short trial. it'll show lower latency and cost but check for any small quality delta — we have eval harness to do that.
[06:03] Aisha: about streaming — our UI expects a first-response within 300ms for perceived performance. is streaming supported in the SDK currently?
[06:10] Daniel: yes, the SDK supports chunked streaming and a handler pattern. note: streaming changes how you do function calls (you might buffer the function output), and structured JSON on stream needs a framing protocol — we supply a small helper to reassemble.
[06:25] Linda: errors and retries — what's recommended?
[06:28] Maya: exponential backoff for transient 5xx, immediate fail for 4xx. for function/tool call errors, we recommend a circuit-breaker per-route and a deterministic fallback like returning last-known-good or marking for manual review.
[06:42] Aisha: ok that maps to our current patterns. a small nit: our typed parser thrown because sometimes the SDK returns timestamps as floats vs ISO strings.
[06:52] Daniel: we'll normalize timestamps in the SDK to ISO by default; we'll add a config flag to accept epoch floats for compatibility.
[07:00] Marco: on telemetry, can we tag traces with our internal request_id so we correlate across systems?
[07:05] Daniel: yes — the SDK accepts a custom header x-internal-request-id and we propagate it into the trace. you can also include a user_id tag.
[07:15] Aisha: great. next — benchmark plan and ramp: we'll need a baseline run on hosted then a Dedicated trial to see p99 stabilization. what's the minimum time for a Dedicated trial?
[07:27] Maya: we can spin a short dedicated pool for 2 weeks as a trial; setup is usually 48–72 hours for provisioning and routing rules.
[07:35] Linda: cost for that trial?
[07:37] Maya: we'll provide a trial pricing line in the follow-up — typically a temporary reserved capacity with credit applied for POC customers.
[07:45] Marco: any compliance blockers for us? we handle payment data; need to understand data residency and retention.
[07:52] Maya: for payment data we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with strict audit/log retention and customer-managed KMS. retention policies configurable per-route. we'll send the compliance checklist.
[08:04] Aisha: can you share structured-output examples for the reconciliation cases — success, partial-match, fail?
[08:11] Maya: yes — we'll post three canonical JSONs in the repo: success (full match with line-items), partial (candidate matches + confidence), fail (error codes, human-review flag).
[08:23] Daniel: quick demo note — in code, the function call handler looks like: 

function handleReconcile(result) {
  // sdk helper normalizes result -> {result, errors, meta} 
  const normalized = SDK.normalize(result);
  if (normalized.errors.length) { // route to review }
}

[08:45] Aisha: looks good. can the SDK auto-retry tool calls idempotently?
[08:50] Daniel: yes if your tool is idempotent. SDK can optionally attach an idempotency key to the tool call; otherwise we recommend the tool side enforce idempotency.
[08:59] Marco: about observability — we want per-route dashboards, and token-level cost breakdowns per model. is that in Redwood Console?
[09:06] Maya: yep Redwood Console exposes per-route model breakdown, token counts, latency histograms and error rates. you can also export raw traces to your analytics.
[09:17] Aisha: ok final quick things: auth — SSO + RBAC for our team?
[09:22] Maya: supported; SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, and role-based access in the Console.
[09:27] Linda: alright, let's recap next steps.
[09:30] Maya: recap: we'll share the sample SDK repo + structured-output JSON + security pack links (Maya). Daniel will run perf tests at 256/512 tokens and post a spreadsheet. Aisha to share payloads and success criteria. we target follow up perf deep-dive next Tue.
[09:48] Marco: cool. any blockers from your side?
[09:50] Aisha: none immediate, just need the repo and the benchmark template.
[09:55] Maya: perfect, we'll get that out today/tomorrow. thanks all.
[10:00] Meeting end.
